questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Convenience and the fact that it is a smaller city where it would be easier for me to connect with the city and the people

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Main thing that could have made it better would be if the link to the institute and local students at the university had been stronger.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was okay, and there was online seminars from the university and the Studierendenwerk (student housing etc.) where most was very thoroughly explained. I had to contact them after to get the full answers I needed, but they usually answered quickly.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The Studierendenwerk put my key in a key box for me to pick it up when I arrived late at night and outside of the Hausmeister's opening hours.
There was a orientation days at the university the week after.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Im Neuenheimer Feld (the science/medicine campus area), there are many student dorms and student WG's (shared appartments). I lived in a 4-person WG

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Shared kitchen within my shared WG. Zentral-Mensa in the middle of the campus area offers quite cheap lunch buffet for students.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Heidelberg is very small so no matter where you live you will be relatively close to your friends as well as your campus. Living on the science campus is practical if you study science of course.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was really happy with my room. Based on my experience with my friends' rooms, some of the rooms are not very beautiful and you might have to buy utensils etc. when you move in, but all rooms are furnished and there are many options for living even right in the middle of the old town, which is quite impressive.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You need to apply in the digital uni system HeiCo after getting accepted

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Emails with a guide on how to apply - it was pretty automatic.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I could apply for any course I wanted on the faculty since they did not need any specific application process. In that sense it was simple.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Regarding being registered as a student: Follow the application guide. Regarding the course registration: Be patient. In Heidelberg, the course catalogue of the semester comes out very late and most students don't know which courses and exams they are taking until the middle of the semester, which can be stressful since it is very different from the process at UCPH. Don't try to plan your courses too perfectly before the semester starts, since you might need to redo the planning anyway if the courses you wanted are not actually being offered - you might end up wasting your energy.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Quite similar level to the courses I would have taken at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Quite similar level to the courses I would have taken at UCPH. But you usually get implicit or explicit "credit points" for showing up and doing bonus assignments during the semester, so it might pay off for the exam if the professor knows who you are.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Mathematical modelling in medicine
Decision-making under cognitive constraints
Computational macroeconomics
Introduction to philosophy (German language course at the ISZ)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The German language course can be a nice way to do something different and still get extra ECTS points.
Both economics courses were nice as well and not too difficult.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: No big ones.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transportation can be a bit expensive if you don't have a bike or a monthly Deutschland-ticket. So get one of those.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university sports is a great and cheap way to do some exercise, especially if you live close to the science campus. Might also be an opportunity to meet new people. You can also sign up for a tandem language partner in order to meet German students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: University sports was very nice, and more social and cheaper than just getting a regular gym membership.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: If you get a Deutschland-ticket, you can travel with all regional/local trains, which makes it "free" to go on one-day trips to all the towns and cities close to Heidelberg. I would definitely do that.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The local culture was not that different from the Danish culture, so quite easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The Erasmus Student Network (ESN) also does a lot of events in the beginning of the semester. Go to as many events as possible even though it can be taxing in the beginning. Then slowly you find your friends and can start relaxing.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The German culture is similar to the Danish, so not that challenging.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Heidelberg is not a busy city, and generally everyone seem more patient and relaxed than in CPH. People are better at just spontaneously sitting down by the river and doing nothing on their way home from uni or work.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Get a D-ticket for months with not a lot of uni and make sure you use it by going on one-day trips 
2. Join the ESN at the beginning and make sure you meet a lot of people
3. There are specific social whatsapp groupchats for f.i. rave events and hiking trips - join them to make sure you know what's going on, since just going out in the Heidelberg Altstadt can quickly get a bit boring

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure you get around the city instead of just visiting the same bars over and over. We found hidden gems very late and regretted not getting around a bit more earlier. And since the city is so small and cute, it is quite doable to play the field.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The carefree way of life and the friendships I got from my Erasmus group.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The bureaucratic stuff surrounding the exchange, mainly in the beginning where we needed to find the courses we wanted and wait for them to be accepted by UCPH.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
